title: The restless heart
about: Augustine, a bishop in Roman North Africa, writes the *Confessions* in Latin between 397 and 400, in his forties. He tells his life to God: his boyhood, a night in his sixteenth year when he and some friends rob a pear tree and throw the fruit to hogs, his conversion at Milan at thirty-one, his mother’s death. Then he turns to what he is now, and to memory, time and the opening of Genesis. The English is E. B. Pusey’s of 1838.

view.says: Auden said that the idea of the gratuitous act, done for nothing, first comes up in the *Confessions*, with the pear tree, and is alien to Greek thought. A Christian like Augustine, he wrote, begins ethics with it: an act neither reasonable nor pleasant, a bare assertion of the self as its own master. A man acts from love of self or of God; reasons and appetites come second.
view.quote: Man, that is to say, always acts either self-loving, just for the hell of it, or God-loving, just for the heaven of it
view.source: “Augustus to Augustine” (*The New Republic*, 25 September 1944), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 36–37; the lecture on *Othello* in *Lectures on Shakespeare*, edited by Arthur Kirsch (2000), p. 197
view.checked: Forewords and Afterwords: read in the scan, research/auden/fa.txt, lines 1775-1804 (page 36 ends at line 1775; the running head of page 37 follows). The Othello lecture: quoted in research notes C, section 5 and appendix H3b; the page is from the editor’s note keyed to 197, read in this session in full-text snippets of the archive.org copy (lecturesonshakes00aude). The editor’s note on the term acte gratuit, seen in the same snippets, refers to Forewords and Afterwords 36-37 and The Dyer’s Hand 430-31. The lecture as printed goes on to quote the episode in Pusey’s translation, and the snippets show words 197 to 233 of the second plate’s paragraph (augustine/book-02, block 8) inside that quotation. Examiner: the sentence itself (the act is foreign to Greek thought and first comes up in the Confessions, in the episode of the pear tree) was seen in snippets of the same copy. The quotation after it runs from about word 30 of that paragraph to word 241 and leaves out the paragraph’s last sentence; the next page, 198, begins after it. The book is put together from notes taken by people who heard the lectures, chiefly Alan Ansen (so its preface, in the same snippets). The 23 words of the quotation were checked again against the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, p. 37, and the date of the review against the list of first printings at the back of that book. Finisher: pp. 36 and 37 read again in the scan (fa.txt, lines 1775 to 1804). One word of the paraphrase was turned, alien for foreign, because with the old word the sentence shared a run of five words with the lecture’s sentence as research notes C quote it (section 5). The lecture itself is in no scan on this machine.

lenses.label: Address
lenses.name: apostrophe
lenses.plain: a turning away: the speaker turns from the hearers to speak to someone or something else; here, from the readers to God
lenses.caption: Every sentence here is spoken to one hearer. In 85 words Thou, Thee, Thy and Thyself come thirteen times. Man is he, then us, and there is no I yet. Rhetoric calls speech turned from its audience to someone else apostrophe, and Augustine makes a whole work of it: all thirteen books are said to God. God knows already what Augustine tells him. In Book II he says he tells it before Thee to mine own kind, and in Book XI that he tells it to stir up his own devotion and his readers’, so that all may say the psalm words this passage begins with.
lenses.why: Augustine says why he tells God what God knows: he tells it before God to his own kind, to stir up his devotion and theirs, so that all may say the psalm’s praise.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Apostrophe as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. A count of *Thou*, *Thee*, *Thy*, *Thine* and *Thyself* in the text printed here. Augustine’s own reasons, in [Book II](#/read/augustine/book-02:4) and at the head of [Book XI](#/read/augustine/book-11:0).

lenses.label: Build
lenses.caption: The first sentence is borrowed: two psalm verses, turned from the Lord to Thou. Augustine’s own words begin at And. The second sentence states a wish (would is the Latin vult, wants to), then says three times what man is: a particle of creation, mortal, a sinner. After yet it states the wish again in the same words. The third sentence names who woke the wish: Thou awakest us. Auden’s summary of Augustine’s picture of man has two parts like these: a fallen creature, and a spirit in him that still witnesses to what his life was meant to be, able to love God.
lenses.why: Augustine sets what man is against what man wants, lets the want stand, and gives God as its cause; Auden’s summary of him likewise has man fallen and still able to love God.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. The verses as the King James Bible has them (Psalms 145:3 and 147:5; James 4:6), which the margin of Pusey’s Latin edition names. *Vult* from that edition, with Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *volo*. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 36.

lenses.caption: Pusey’s restless and repose hide a repetition. In Augustine’s Latin they are inquietum, not at rest, and requiescat, comes to rest, both built on quies, rest. So the sentence names rest twice: first as what the heart is without, then as what it comes to in God. For Thyself is ad te, and the first sense of ad is direction, toward. Read that way, God made us toward himself, and the heart is restless until it rests in him. Awakest is excitas, you rouse. At the head of Book XI Augustine uses the same verb of himself: by telling his story he rouses his own devotion and his readers’.
lenses.why: In Latin the heart’s unrest and its rest share one root, and man is made toward God: the sentence names the unrest as the lack of the rest it comes to in him.
lenses.stands: Augustine’s Latin as Pusey’s edition of 1838 prints it, in Book I, chapter 1, and at the head of [Book XI](#/read/augustine/book-11:0). Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *inquietus*, *requiesco*, *quies*, *ad* and *excito*. The lines themselves.

lenses.caption: Pusey’s English has 111,772 words in thirteen books, all spoken to God: a word for Thou comes 2,889 times, about once in 39 words. By Augustine’s own account ten books are about himself and three on the opening of Genesis, as far as the Sabbath rest. Repose in Thee returns in the third paragraph from the end as rest in Thee, the same Latin verb, and there it is still to come, in eternal life. Between them Book IX has the verb with in Thee once: a rest already had, at a friend’s country house. In Book X, on what he is now, he calls himself a burden to himself, because he is not yet full of God.
lenses.why: The rest named in the first paragraph returns on the last pages as something still to come; between them a man who says he is a burden to himself speaks thirteen books to God.
lenses.stands: A count of the words of Pusey’s English as printed here, and in it of *Thou*, *Thee*, *Thy*, *Thine* and *Thyself* with a capital. Augustine’s *Retractations*, Book II, chapter 6, printed at the head of Pusey’s Latin edition, which also gives the verb. The places themselves: [Book IX](#/read/augustine/book-09:4), [Book XIII](#/read/augustine/book-13:49), and in Book X [what he is now](#/read/augustine/book-10:3) and [the burden](#/read/augustine/book-10:38).

lenses.label: Itself
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build; here, three times, a missing motive and the deed
lenses.caption: Three times a clause turns on but, and each time the noun after it takes up the word before it: ill and the ill itself, faulty and my fault itself, the shame and the shame itself. The first half is the place for a motive, and each time it says there was none. Pusey’s temptation is the Latin causa, a cause: his ill had no cause but itself. Two paragraphs later Augustine gives the rule this breaks: nobody believes in a crime done for no cause, and even the conspirator Catiline had one. Auden calls such an act gratuitous and says the idea first comes up here. The repeated nouns are Augustine’s; Pusey adds itself twice.
lenses.why: Three times the passage makes room for a motive and fills it with the deed again: this is the act without a motive that Augustine says nobody believes in and that Auden says first comes up here.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Augustine’s Latin in Pusey’s edition of 1838, Book II, chapter 4, with Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *causa*. The rule about Catiline, two paragraphs later in [Book II](#/read/augustine/book-02:10); that he was a conspirator, the *New English Dictionary* under *Catiline*. Auden: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, p. 197.

lenses.label: Loved
lenses.name: anaphora
lenses.plain: the same words at the head of clause after clause
lenses.caption: I loved heads three clauses. Words repeated at the head of clause after clause are called anaphora. The verb stays the same and its object changes: first it, the ill, then to perish, then mine own fault. The lines give the love and no reason for it. The verb is amavi, the one Augustine uses of his love of God in the passage from Book X. In Auden’s summary of Augustine a man always acts from love of himself or of God, and his reasons and appetites come second. The Latin says amavi a fourth time, closing the next clause; Pusey leaves that one out.
lenses.why: The repeated verb makes the theft an act of love whose object becomes his own ruin; he uses the same verb of God in Book X, and Auden’s summary knows only two loves, of self and of God.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Anaphora as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. *Amavi* in Pusey’s Latin edition of 1838, Book II, chapter 4, and Book X, chapter 27. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 37.

lenses.caption: Gratuitously is Pusey’s word for gratis: for nothing, with no return. Auden’s name for the act told here is the French for a gratuitous act, acte gratuit. Gratis is a form of gratia, favor, the word that gives English grace. Augustine uses both. Six paragraphs later he ascribes to God’s gratia his pardon and the evil he did not do, and he calls the crime he loved gratuitum. So his Latin names the crime and the grace from one root. Pusey loses the pair there: he writes a sin for its own sake. Fault is defectus, a defection or a lack, and Augustine says later that the theft he loved was nothing.
lenses.why: Augustine’s word for his crime, gratis, is a form of his word for grace, and his word for what he loved means a lack: the act is done for nothing and, as he says later, was nothing.
lenses.stands: Augustine’s Latin in Pusey’s edition of 1838, Book II, chapters 4 and 7. Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *gratia*, *gratuitus* and *defectus*; the Online Etymology Dictionary under *gratis* and *grace*. His later words in Book II on [grace](#/read/augustine/book-02:14) and on [nothing](#/read/augustine/book-02:15). Auden: *Lectures on Shakespeare*, p. 197, and *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 36–37.

lenses.caption: Book II has 3,781 words, and the theft takes 78 of them. In the 1,945 words after it, just over half the book, he examines what he loved in it, with 33 question marks. Auden told his 1941 class that Augustine’s account of the conflict between self and ego is the earliest classic of self-analysis. One answer Augustine tries, five paragraphs later, is that he was a prisoner imitating freedom: he did unpunished what was forbidden, a dim likeness of God’s power. Auden says why so many gratuitous acts, Augustine’s among them, are crimes: by breaking a law a man asserts that he is free. The last paragraph asks who can untie the knot.
lenses.why: The theft gets 78 words; in the 1,945 after it he examines it, so the weight is on the motive. Auden called Augustine’s account the earliest classic of self-analysis; his reason for such crimes is one Augustine tries here.
lenses.stands: A count of words and question marks in Book II as printed here. Donald Pearce’s notes of Auden’s lecture, in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, p. 134. Two later places in Book II: [the prisoner](#/read/augustine/book-02:13) and [the knot](#/read/augustine/book-02:17). Auden: *The Dyer’s Hand*, p. 430, and “Squares and Oblongs,” in *Poets at Work*, pp. 167–68.

lenses.caption: Too late is one Latin word, sero. Loved is amavi, the verb of the theft in the passage from Book II. Augustine uses the same verb for both loves, and so does Auden’s summary of him. Within is intus, inside, and abroad is foris, out of doors. The beautiful things are formosa, finely formed, and he is deformis, misshapen, both from forma, shape. Pusey keeps the pair in deformed and forms. The things stay beautiful, and God made them. What is wrong is where he looks and what he is. Auden notes that the doctrine Augustine held finds nothing in matter evil in itself.
lenses.why: The Latin pairs inside with outside and the finely formed with the misshapen, so the fault lies in where he looks and what he is; the things stay beautiful, and Auden notes this doctrine finds nothing in matter evil.

lenses.label: Crossing
lenses.name: chiasmus
lenses.plain: a crossing: two things are named, then named again in the opposite order
lenses.caption: One short sentence names the two persons twice, in opposite order: Thou, me, then I, Thee. This crossing is called chiasmus. The word that joins each pair is the same, with, and the second half adds not. So one relation is said twice, and it holds in one direction and fails in the other. It is not a matter of place: the paragraph before says Place there is none. Auden, setting out the doctrine Augustine held, says the love it means is a relation that goes both ways. Here the way from Augustine to God is missing. The crossing is Augustine’s: mecum eras, et tecum non eram.
lenses.why: The sentence crosses the two persons around one word, with, and denies it in one direction only; the love Auden says this doctrine means goes both ways, and the missing way is Augustine’s.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Chiasmus as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. The paragraph before, in [Book X](#/read/augustine/book-10:36), and the Latin of the sentence from Pusey’s edition of 1838. Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, pp. 35–36.

lenses.label: Senses
lenses.name: enumeration
lenses.plain: a counting out: one thing told part by part; here, sense by sense
lenses.caption: The last five sentences count out the five senses, one each: hearing, sight, smell, taste, touch. Thirty paragraphs earlier Augustine asks what he loves when he loves God, and answers with the same five, known inwardly: a light, a melody, a fragrance, a food, an embrace. There sight comes first. Here hearing does, with Thou calledst. The earlier paragraph says how his love began: God struck his heart with his word, and without God’s mercy heaven and earth speak to deaf ears. Three paragraphs after this passage he starts on what still tempts him and takes the senses in turn again: first sexual desire, then food and drink, smells, sounds and sights.
lenses.why: Each sense gets a sentence, hearing first; by his own account the love began when God’s word struck his heart, and Book X counts by the senses both what he loves in God and what still tempts him.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Two other places in Book X: [what he loves when he loves God](#/read/augustine/book-10:7), thirty paragraphs earlier, and his review of what still tempts him, which [begins](#/read/augustine/book-10:40) three paragraphs later and ends with [the eyes](#/read/augustine/book-10:50).

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: The marks show who acts. In the first two marked sentences every verb is God’s, six of them, each with the old ending -st that goes with Thou. Then Augustine’s verbs come in, as answers: God breathes and he draws breath, God touches and he burns. One sentence has no Thou: I tasted, and hunger and thirst. Its last two verbs are in the present tense, as panted is in the Latin. The hunger goes on as he writes. Two paragraphs later he asks God to act first again: Give what Thou enjoinest. Auden set the prayer’s Latin in New Year Letter (1941), with a note to Book X.
lenses.why: God’s verbs come first and Augustine’s follow as answers; the one sentence that is all his ends in the present tense: he hungers as he writes, and two paragraphs later he asks God to give what he commands.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the lines themselves. Two other places in Book X: [what he is now](#/read/augustine/book-10:3) and [the prayer](#/read/augustine/book-10:39). The Latin verbs from Pusey’s edition of 1838, Book X, chapter 27. Auden: *New Year Letter* (1941), line 1684 and his note to it.

auden.says: A student in the 1941 class, Donald Pearce, wrote down part of a lecture on the ego in Augustine and Kafka. Auden called what Augustine wrote on the conflict between self and ego the earliest classic of self-analysis. Since Freud, he went on, the ego no longer looks like the single, steady thing it was for Augustine, so the account now matters less as psychology than as ethics, where he said it will always be a founding text.
auden.quote: the subtlest introspectionist between Aristotle and Freud
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), p. 134

auden.says: In his review of 1944 Auden sets out what Augustine put in place of the classical picture of man. Man is made in God’s image, and is fallen. The dividing line runs between a self-loving state of all his powers, of body and of mind, and a spirit in him that still witnesses to what his life was meant to be, able to love God as God loves him. Nothing in matter is evil in itself, and the love meant is a relation that goes both ways.
auden.source: “Augustus to Augustine,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 35–36

auden.says: Many gratuitous acts are crimes, Auden wrote, and he gave the reason. People want to be free and also to feel that they matter. By breaking a law a man asserts that he is free, and since it is a weighty law he still feels that he matters. In an essay printed in 1948 he says the same and gives Augustine’s act as the example. There he credits Augustine with being the first to see that man in his natural state hates nature, and that only an act done for nothing can content him.
auden.source: “Postscript: The Frivolous & The Earnest,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 430; “Squares and Oblongs,” in *Poets at Work* (1948), pp. 167–68

caveats: Only Auden’s words on the pear tree are about a passage shown here. What comes from his essay of 1944, a review of C. N. Cochrane’s *Christianity and Classical Culture*, sums up Augustine’s teaching as that book sets it out. It is not said of these passages.

Auden’s lecture on *Othello* survives in notes taken by people who heard it. That lecture, “Squares and Oblongs” and *New Year Letter* were read here only in snippets of scanned copies. The 1941 lecture on Augustine and Kafka is known from a student’s notes, which do not name the *Confessions*.

Auden’s course assigned the Loeb edition, with William Watts’s English of 1631. The English here is Pusey’s as Project Gutenberg prints it. In the third passage it reads *panted*, where Pusey’s first printing and the Latin have the present, *pant*.

*Ad te*, glossed here as *toward you*, can also be taken as *for you*, which is how Pusey has it. Apostrophe usually names a turn made inside a speech; calling the whole book one rests on Augustine’s saying that he tells his story to his own kind.
The counts are of Pusey’s English, not of the Latin. The words for *Thou* are every *Thou*, *Thee*, *Thy*, *Thine* and *Thyself* with a capital, and at least two of the 2,889 are not said to God.
